sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Padmasambhava** ​(*padmasambhava*) — ‌Lotus-Born, Vajrayana, ‌Tibet · ​'Lotus-born' (padma ​'lotus' + ​sambhava ​'born, arisen'), ​'Guru Rinpoche', ‌the tantric ​master revered ​as the ‌founder-figure ​of Tibetan ‌Buddhism. — ​belongs to ‌the Buddhist ​tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Lotus-Born, ‌Vajrayana, Tibet". ​The ‌name means ​"'Lotus-born' (padma ‌'lotus' + ​sambhava 'born, ‌arisen'), 'Guru ​Rinpoche', ‌the tantric ​master revered ​as the ‌founder-figure of ‌Tibetan Buddhism."[^1].

‌**Padmasambhava** ​— the ​**Lotus-Born**, revered ‌across the ​Tibetan world ​as **Guru ‌Rinpoche**, ​'Precious Teacher' ​— is ‌the tantric ​master credited ‌with **planting ​Buddhism ​in Tibet**: ​taming its ​spirits, raising ‌its first ‌monastery, and ​hiding ‌its deepest ​teachings as ​treasures for ‌future ages.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the ‌canonical scholarly ​spelling **Padmasambhava** ‌and serves ​its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/padmasambhava/). ‌The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed form ​itself. The ‌plain ASCII ​form *padmasambhava* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: no ​recovered diacritics ‌or special ‌encoding is ​claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Devanagari as ​**पद्मसम्भव**. Etymologically ​it ​means "'Lotus-born' ​(padma 'lotus' ​+ sambhava ‌'born, arisen'), ​'Guru Rinpoche', ​the ‌tantric master ​revered as ‌the founder-figure ​of Tibetan ‌Buddhism."[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling **Padmasambhava** ​matches the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. The ‌plain ​ASCII form ‌*padmasambhava* contains ​the same ‌letters, so ​no ‌lost diacritics ​or encoding ‌transition is ​claimed. The ​editorial work ‌is ‌to fix ‌one reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve capitalization ‌and ​provenance, and ​keep the ‌original evidence ​visible. The ​displayed form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form ​itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- **p** ​→ **P** ‌— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**a** → ‌**a** — ‌Same
- **d** ‌→ **d** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/padmasambhava/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**padmasambhava** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Padmasambhava.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Padmasambhava" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Padmasambhava" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"padmasambhava" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Padmasambhava ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Padmasambhava ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Padmasambhava ‌place lotus-born, ​vajrayana, tibet ​at ​the center ​of ​a living ‌mythological ​world.

### Origins ​(Myth)

‌Padmasambhava appears ​in buddhist ‌tradition ​as lotus-born, ‌vajrayana, ​tibet. The ​name's ​meaning, "'Lotus-born' ​(padma ​'lotus' + ‌sambhava 'born, ​arisen'), ‌'Guru Rinpoche', ​the ‌tantric master ​revered ‌as the ​founder-figure ‌of Tibetan ​Buddhism.", shapes ​the ‌narratives told ‌about ‌this figure.

### ​Worship ​and Memory ‌(Cult)

​Devotees and ​later tradition-keepers ‌preserved ​Padmasambhava in ​ritual, ‌text, and ​iconography, ‌ensuring the ​name ​survived into ​the modern ​scholarly ‌record.

The ‌myths ​of Padmasambhava ‌survive ​in fragments, ​summaries, ‌and later ‌retellings. Each ‌version ‌reflects the ​interests ‌of its ​tellers ​— poets, ​priests, ‌philosophers, and ​scholars. The ​PuniCodex ​entry does ‌not ​privilege a ​single ​version; it ‌gathers ​the attestations ‌so that ​readers ‌can compare ​them. ‌The restoration ‌Padmasambhava ​gives the ​figure ​a stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Padmasambhava ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Buddhist ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌पद्मसम्भव, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​lotus-born ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Padmasambhava is ​the founder ‌who refuses ‌to be ​historical — ​and that ​refusal is ​his deepest ​teaching. The tradition ‌does not ​ask you ​to believe ‌a man ​was born ‌on a ​lotus; it ‌asks you to ​notice what ​the image ​does: a ​teacher with ​no parents, ‌no caste, ​no homeland, ‌arriving from the ​pure lake ‌the way ​insight arrives ‌from nowhere. ​The 14th ‌century wrote ​his 8th-century ​life, and no ‌one calls ‌it fraud, ‌because the ​figure was ​designed for ‌exactly this ​— a ​founder whose biography ‌is a ​**treasure-text**, to ​be discovered, ‌not verified.

​His practical ‌legacy is ​the taming: ​Buddhism did not ​conquer Tibet ​by argument ‌alone but ‌by converting ​the landscape ‌— the ​old gods ​stayed, renamed and ‌re-employed. It ‌is the ‌most successful ‌model of ​cultural transmission ‌ever devised: ​nothing destroyed, ​everything bound to ​the vow. ‌And his ​final act ​— burying ​the teaching ‌— is ​the strangest ​bequest in religious ​history: a ‌gift addressed ​to the ‌future, with ​the Guru's ‌certainty that ​the future ‌would deserve it ‌and would ​know where ​to dig. ​Every crisis ​of Tibetan ‌Buddhism since ‌has proven ​him right.[^1]
